guide.title: Richmond Hill, Queens: A National Register District, the El and Little Guyana
guide.intro: Richmond Hill is a Queens neighborhood in Community District 9, filed by the Department of City Planning as the tabulation area QN0902 inside QN09 Kew Gardens-Richmond Hill-Woodhaven, alongside QN0901 Kew Gardens and QN0903 South Richmond Hill. The area borders Kew Gardens and Forest Park to the north, Jamaica and South Jamaica to the east, South Ozone Park to the south, and Woodhaven and Ozone Park to the west, and the portion south of Atlantic Avenue is also known as South Richmond Hill. The Richmond Hill Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places, takes in 200 contributing buildings raised between 1890 and 1915 beside the former South Side Railroad line, now the Long Island Rail Road's Montauk Branch. The elevated BMT Jamaica Line runs above Jamaica Avenue here, with stations at 121st Street, 111th Street and 104th Street, and the Van Wyck Expressway forms the eastern edge.

sections.heading: The historic district and the landmarks
sections.body:
The Richmond Hill Historic District is a National Register of Historic Places listing, nomination number 100003430. It takes in 200 contributing buildings raised between 1890 and 1915 beside the former South Side Railroad line — now the Long Island Rail Road's Montauk Branch — and the Richmond Hill station at Hillside Avenue, and its outline is roughly a triangle. Its National Register cover sheet gives the district two ZIP codes, 11415 and 11418. Wikipedia's article on the district calls the dominant architecture the Shingle style, with many houses in an earlier style called the Stick style.

The district's northern tier follows 84th Avenue, the original Division Avenue, and that line is also the Kew Gardens boundary, so a house can stand inside the district and inside Kew Gardens' tabulation area at once. The nomination singles out a pair of houses by the builders Wade & Cullingford on that northern seam. The contributing houses are private single-family residences.

The architect Henry Edward Haugaard opened an office in the neighborhood in 1888, which the Landmarks Preservation Commission's designation report LP-2126 puts at Jamaica Plank Road and Lefferts Boulevard and the National Register nomination at Jamaica Avenue and Lefferts Boulevard. The two records disagree about the man as well: LP-2126 says he was born in 1867 in Brooklyn, while the nomination gives his dates as 1866–1939. LP-2126 records that the architectural legacy continued into the next generation with two of the Haugaard sons: William E. Haugaard became New York State Architect in 1928, and John T. Haugaard Jr. worked as Senior Housing Control Architect and Associate Architect for the State of New York.

Individual New York City landmark designations cover the Richmond Hill Republican Club at 86-15 Lefferts Boulevard, which LP-2126 calls an integral part of downtown Richmond Hill; Public School 66 at 85-11 102nd Street, which LP-2317 places in east central Queens, in the neighborhood of Richmond Hill; and the Eldridge House at 87-61 111th Street, covered by LP-2473. The Landmarks Preservation Commission has designated no historic district in Richmond Hill.

The Church of the Resurrection, a historic Episcopal church and rectory at 85-09 118th Street, was built in 1874 on land donated by the Man estate, just east of the historic district; the Richmond Hill article puts it on the neighborhood's northern edge. Its ZIP code is 11415, which is also Kew Gardens' code and one of the two the district's cover sheet carries. Holy Child Jesus stands at 111-11 86th Avenue. St. Benedict Joseph Labre Parish is at 94-40 118th Street. The Richmond Hill Historical Society is at 112-13 84th Avenue, inside the district. Wikipedia's list of the neighborhood's notable residents places Jack Kerouac here from 1950 to 1955.

sections.heading: Liberty Avenue, 101st Avenue and South Richmond Hill
sections.body:
The portion of the neighborhood south of Atlantic Avenue is also known as South Richmond Hill. Liberty Avenue, an 8-mile (13 km) west-east avenue in Brooklyn and Queens, runs through it. Wikipedia records that the avenue was co-named "Little Guyana Avenue" on May 29, 2021, and that the MTA put up a "Welcome to Little Guyana" sign in early 2024. 101st Avenue is known by the name Little Punjab; a second Wikipedia article gives the name as Punjab Avenue. Wikipedia also records the co-namings James J. Creegan Square and Felix Cuervo Corner.

LP-2126 describes the neighborhood's change of population — a population of mostly German and Irish descent gave way to an influx of Latin Americans — and adds that Richmond Hill remains a low-rise neighborhood of two-family houses and apartment buildings. A Community District 9 figure, covering Kew Gardens and Woodhaven along with Richmond Hill, puts the district at eleven bodegas for every supermarket.

Phil "Scooter" Rizzuto Park is at 125-02 Atlantic Avenue, filed by NYC Parks under two ZIP codes, 11418 and 11419. McConnell Park is NYC Parks property Q217, and the agency's history page for it says the park is located in Richmond Hill; Parks gives its extent as "94 Ave., Atlantic Ave. bet. Leffers Blvd. and 120 St." — the dataset's own spelling of Lefferts — and its acreage as 0.207 in Parks Properties against 0.21 on its own page. Parks files the park in council district 29, while Wikipedia gives the neighborhood's council districts as 28, 30 and 32. Standing at Atlantic Avenue and Lefferts Boulevard is the Morris Park World War Memorial, a stele with two tablets in bronze and Deer Island granite by the architect H. Adler, which Parks records as dedicated in 1923 and again in 1973, with a new plaque given by Lt. F. J. McConnell Post No. 229, V.F.W. Parks' monument record titles it the Morris Park World War Memorial; the agency's own McConnell history page calls it the Morris Park World War I Memorial.

The NYPD's 102nd Precinct station house is at 87-34 118th Street, and the command patrols Kew Gardens, Richmond Hill and Woodhaven. FDNY Engine Company 294 and Ladder Company 143 are at 101-02 Jamaica Avenue, and Squad 270 with Division 13 at 91-45 121st Street. The United States Post Office's Richmond Hill Station is at 122-01 Jamaica Avenue, the Queens Public Library's Richmond Hill branch at 118-14 Hillside Avenue, and Richmond Hill High School at 89-30 114th Street.

Between Myrtle Avenue and the Montauk Line railroad stands a former movie theatre at 117-09 Hillside Avenue, opened in 1929, which Wikipedia records has functioned since 1968 as a bingo hall. Its own article titles it RKO Keith's Theater, while the neighborhood's article and the historic district's article both call it RKO Keith's Richmond Hill Theater. Wikipedia also records that it is on the State Register only, the property owner having refused listing on the National Register.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The elevated BMT Jamaica Line runs above Jamaica Avenue through Richmond Hill, along with Woodhaven and the Cypress Hills section of Brooklyn. Its 121st Street station is at the intersection of 121st Street and Jamaica Avenue, in Richmond Hill and Kew Gardens. Its 111th Street station is in Richmond Hill and is served at all times by the J train. Its 104th Street station is on Jamaica Avenue between 102nd and 104th Streets, in Richmond Hill.

The Long Island Rail Road's Montauk Branch crosses the neighborhood on a viaduct, and the Richmond Hill station sits on it. The station opened in 1868 under the name Clarenceville Station, and that name was changed in 1871. Its location is given differently by different articles: the neighborhood's own article puts it on Hillside Avenue and Babbage Street; the station's article describes it at Myrtle Avenue, cutting diagonally from the intersection of Jamaica Avenue and Lefferts Boulevard through to Hillside Avenue; and the Clarenceville station article places it at Jamaica Avenue and Lefferts Boulevard. It is distinct from the Clarenceville station on the Atlantic Branch, which stood on Atlantic Avenue west of 111th Street in the Richmond Hill section of Queens.

The Van Wyck Expressway forms Richmond Hill's eastern edge, and the Jamaica–Van Wyck station stands on the expressway and carries Jamaica in its name. Lefferts Boulevard runs through the communities of Kew Gardens, Richmond Hill and South Ozone Park. Liberty Avenue runs west to east for 8 miles (13 km) across Brooklyn and Queens, and Jamaica Avenue is fronted by Richmond Hill and by Jamaica alike.

faq.question: How do I get to Richmond Hill?
faq.answer: By subway, the elevated BMT Jamaica Line runs above Jamaica Avenue through the neighborhood. Its 121st Street station is at the intersection of 121st Street and Jamaica Avenue, in Richmond Hill and Kew Gardens; its 111th Street station is in Richmond Hill and is served at all times by the J train; and its 104th Street station is on Jamaica Avenue between 102nd and 104th Streets. By rail, the Long Island Rail Road's Montauk Branch crosses the neighborhood on a viaduct and carries the Richmond Hill station, which opened in 1868 as Clarenceville Station and was renamed in 1871. By road, the Van Wyck Expressway forms the eastern edge, and Lefferts Boulevard runs through Kew Gardens, Richmond Hill and South Ozone Park.

faq.question: What is the Richmond Hill Historic District?
faq.answer: A National Register of Historic Places district, nomination number 100003430. It takes in 200 contributing buildings raised between 1890 and 1915 beside the former South Side Railroad line — now the Long Island Rail Road's Montauk Branch — and the Richmond Hill station at Hillside Avenue, and its outline is roughly a triangle. Its cover sheet gives the district two ZIP codes, 11415 and 11418. Its northern tier follows 84th Avenue, the original Division Avenue, which is also the Kew Gardens boundary, so a house can stand inside the district and inside Kew Gardens' tabulation area at once. The contributing houses are private single-family residences. The Landmarks Preservation Commission has designated no historic district here, though it has designated individual landmarks.

faq.question: Is South Richmond Hill part of Richmond Hill?
faq.answer: The portion of the neighborhood south of Atlantic Avenue is also known as South Richmond Hill. The Department of City Planning tabulates it separately as QN0903 South Richmond Hill, alongside QN0902 Richmond Hill and QN0901 Kew Gardens, all three inside QN09 Kew Gardens-Richmond Hill-Woodhaven. St. Benedict Joseph Labre Parish at 94-40 118th Street and Phil "Scooter" Rizzuto Park at 125-02 Atlantic Avenue both fall in that southern part; NYC Parks files the park under both 11418 and 11419.

faq.question: Which neighborhood is the Church of the Resurrection in?
faq.answer: Richmond Hill. The church's own article opens by calling it a historic Episcopal church and rectory in Richmond Hill, Queens, and Wikipedia's Richmond Hill article says the northern edge of Richmond Hill contains it. Its ZIP code, 11415, is also Kew Gardens' code, and the National Register table lists the church under both neighborhood names — but the Richmond Hill Historic District's own cover sheet gives the district both 11415 and 11418. The National Register nomination puts the building on land donated by the Man estate in 1874, just east of the historic district.

faq.question: Did the 1950 Long Island Rail Road crash happen in Richmond Hill?
faq.answer: No. The account of the crash puts the collision outside Richmond Hill. What ties the neighborhood's name to it is a second name: the same account records that the disaster is also known as the Richmond Hill disaster. The name is the connection; the crash site is not in this neighborhood.

photos.title: Jamaica Avenue under the elevated
photos.description: The roadway runs away between rows of teal-painted steel columns that carry the elevated railway overhead on riveted plate girders and latticed cross-bracing, with green traffic signals hung from brackets beneath the deck. Orange-and-white barrels and barricades line both curbs and a white contractor's trailer sits at the left curb. The brick building behind it carries stacked signboards for an exterminator, a window and gutter installer and a beauty center; a green street sign to the right reads 121 St, and red scaffolding rises against a building beyond it.
photos.author: Tdorante10

places.name: Richmond Hill Republican Club
places.summary: A building at 86-15 Lefferts Boulevard covered by Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report LP-2126, which calls it an integral part of downtown Richmond Hill.

photos.title: The pediment and cornice
photos.description: A triangular pediment rises above the roofline, its white field carrying raised dark letters that read REPUBLICAN CLUB, with the paint flaked away in patches around them. A white cornice runs the width of the front on scrolled brackets set over a course of small dentils. The wall below is buff brick, divided into bays by white fluted pilasters whose capitals end in paired scrolls. A pipe railing crosses the roof behind the pediment, and a leafy branch reaches in from the right against a blue sky.
photos.author: Peter Greenberg

places.name: Public School 66
places.summary: A school building at 85-11 102nd Street covered by Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report LP-2317, which places it in east central Queens, in the neighborhood of Richmond Hill. The National Register's Queens table lists it under the city name Richmond Hill.

places.name: Eldridge House
places.summary: A house covered by Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report LP-2473, whose header gives the address as 87-61 111th Street. The Commission's Individual Landmark Sites dataset spells the street "111st Street"; the designation report's spelling is the one to use.

places.name: Church of the Resurrection
places.summary: A historic Episcopal church and rectory at 85-09 118th Street, which Wikipedia's Richmond Hill article places on the northern edge of the neighborhood. Its ZIP code, 11415, is also Kew Gardens' code; the Richmond Hill Historic District's National Register cover sheet gives the district both 11415 and 11418.
places.history: The church was built in 1874 on land donated by the Man estate, just east of the historic district.

photos.title: The church from the sidewalk
photos.description: A steeply pitched gable faces the street, its cream stucco panels crossed by dark timbering and a wooden cross standing at the peak. Tall pointed-arch windows fill the gable above the sweep of a lower porch roof. The walls beneath are rough dark fieldstone laid up with pale mortar, with stained-glass lancet windows and wooden doors set under the eaves, and a black notice board gives service times and a welcome in English and Spanish. A square stone tower at the right carries a green copper spire above louvered belfry openings. A clipped hedge runs along the front and the trees around the building are bare.
photos.author: Peter Greenberg

places.name: McConnell Park
places.summary: NYC Parks property Q217, whose extent the agency gives as "94 Ave., Atlantic Ave. bet. Leffers Blvd. and 120 St." — the dataset's own spelling of Lefferts. Parks' history page for the park says the park is located in Richmond Hill.

places.name: Morris Park World War Memorial
places.summary: A war memorial at Atlantic Avenue and Lefferts Boulevard, recorded by NYC Parks as a stele with two tablets, in bronze and Deer Island granite, by the architect H. Adler. Parks records it as dedicated in 1923 and again in 1973, with a new plaque given by Lt. F. J. McConnell Post No. 229, V.F.W. The agency's monument record titles it the Morris Park World War Memorial; its own McConnell Park history page calls it the Morris Park World War I Memorial.
places.history: The first plaque is inscribed "DEDICATED / TO THE SONS OF MORRIS PARK AND / VICINITY WHO SERVED IN THE / WORLD WAR -1917-18 AND IN LOVING / REMEMBRANCE OF THE FOLLOWING / MEN WHO MADE THE SUPREME SACRIFICE". The second carries an eagle and the V.F.W. seal above the words "WITH UNDYING LOVE / AND GRATITUDE".

places.summary: A former movie theatre at 117-09 Hillside Avenue, between Myrtle Avenue and the Montauk Line railroad, opened in 1929. Wikipedia records that it has functioned since 1968 as a bingo hall. Its own article titles it RKO Keith's Theater; the neighborhood's article and the historic district's article both call it RKO Keith's Richmond Hill Theater.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the building is on the State Register only, the property owner having refused listing on the National Register.
